prompt.context: Your client is a $2B hedge fund. Previously they selected investments based on a complex mathematical model. However, about 2 years ago they started seeing lower returns. To address this problem they added a research team to help evaluate investments. If the model recommends an investment, money is invested. If the model and the analysts agree on an investment, a larger percentage is invested than if only the model recommends the investment. The research team consists of 4 Senior Analysts and 3 Junior Analysts. The CEO is extremely pleased with the new research team and the uplift in returns they have seen as a result of the new investment methodology. However, he does not feel that the team is properly structured and has asked you to advise him on structuring the team.
prompt.question: What issues would you consider and how would you structure the team?

clarifying_info.q: What is the overall goal of the hedge fund?
clarifying_info.a: To maximize returns; they tolerate a high amount of risk.

clarifying_info.q: How much do individual investors invest?
Who do the researchers currently report to?
clarifying_info.a: All seven researchers currently report to the head of trading.

clarifying_info.q: How does work currently flow to the research team?
clarifying_info.a: When the trading department has a question on an investment, the head of trading contacts one of the Senior Analysts and asks him to evaluate an investment. The Senior Analyst then prioritizes the request and divides it between himself/herself and the Junior Analysts.

clarifying_info.q: Can investment research be broken into discrete pieces?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, investment research (even an individual request) can usually be broken into several discrete pieces.

clarifying_info.q: Is the CEO open to letting people go?
clarifying_info.a: The CEO does not want to fire anyone.

clarifying_info.q: Are analysts satisfied with their current work?
clarifying_info.a: Both Junior and Senior analysts feel that they are doing work that is beneath them.

exhibits.title: Work Allocation by Role and Task Type
exhibits.shows: A table showing how research work is divided among Senior Analysts, Junior Analysts, and Research Assistants across three task types (Data Gathering, Analysis, Synthesis), and a second table showing the percentage breakdown of total research hours by task type.

framework: Compensation and rewards structure — how to incentivize each level of analyst appropriately
Reporting lines — who reports to whom and whether the current structure (all reporting to head of trading) is optimal
Appropriate leverage — what is the right ratio of Senior Analysts to Junior Analysts to Research Assistants to maximize efficiency and avoid under/over-utilization

questions.prompt: Using the exhibit data, calculate how many hours each type of worker contributes per 100 hours of research work if work is pushed to the lowest competent level.
questions.guidance: Apply the percentage splits from the exhibit. For each task, multiply total hours by each role's share. Sum across tasks for each role.

math.setup: 100 total research hours split: Data Gathering = 20 hrs, Analysis = 60 hrs, Synthesis = 20 hrs. For each task, apply the role-level splits from the exhibit.
steps: Data Gathering (20 hrs): Sr. Analyst = 20 × 25% = 5 hrs; Jr. Analyst = 20 × 25% = 5 hrs; Assistant = 20 × 50% = 10 hrs
Analysis (60 hrs): Sr. Analyst = 60 × 20% = 12 hrs; Jr. Analyst = 60 × 80% = 48 hrs; Assistant = 60 × 0% = 0 hrs
Synthesis (20 hrs): Sr. Analyst = 20 × 80% = 16 hrs; Jr. Analyst = 20 × 20% = 4 hrs; Assistant = 20 × 0% = 0 hrs
Total per role: Sr. Analyst = 5 + 12 + 16 = 33 hrs; Jr. Analyst = 5 + 48 + 4 = 57 hrs; Assistant = 10 + 0 + 0 = 10 hrs
math.answer: Per 100 hours of research: Senior Analyst contributes 33 hrs, Junior Analyst 57 hrs, Research Assistant 10 hrs.

questions.prompt: Based on the hours per role, what is the appropriate ratio of Senior Analysts to Junior Analysts to Research Assistants?
questions.guidance: Divide each role's hours by the Senior Analyst hours to find the leverage ratio relative to one Senior Analyst.

math.setup: Sr. Analyst = 33 hrs, Jr. Analyst = 57 hrs, Assistant = 10 hrs per 100-hour project.
steps: Ratio of Jr. Analysts to Sr. Analysts: 57 / 33 ≈ 1.7, roughly 2 Jr. Analysts per Sr. Analyst
Ratio of Assistants to Sr. Analysts: 10 / 33 ≈ 0.3, roughly 1 assistant shared among 3 Sr. Analysts
math.answer: 1 Senior Analyst : ~2 Junior Analysts : ~0.33 Research Assistants (i.e., 1 assistant shared across 3 Senior Analysts).

questions.prompt: Given 4 Senior Analysts, recommend the new organizational structure.
questions.guidance: Scale the ratio. 4 Sr. Analysts × 2 Jr. Analysts each = 8 Jr. Analysts; 4 Sr. Analysts / 3 per assistant ≈ 1.33, so ~1–2 shared Research Assistants. Currently there are only 3 Jr. Analysts, so the client needs to hire 5 more Jr. Analysts and add Research Assistants. Each Sr. Analyst leads a pod of 2 Jr. Analysts; assistants are a shared resource.

math.setup: 4 Sr. Analysts; ratio is 1 Sr. : 2 Jr. : 0.33 Asst.
steps: Jr. Analysts needed: 4 × 2 = 8 (currently have 3, need to add 5)
Assistants needed: 4 / 3 ≈ 1.33, round to 1–2 shared assistants (none currently)
math.answer: 4 pods each with 1 Sr. Analyst + 2 Jr. Analysts, plus 1–2 shared Research Assistants (total: 4 Sr., 8 Jr., ~2 Asst.).

brainstorming.prompt: What additional implications or considerations arise from restructuring the team this way?

categories.name: Utilization and capacity
ideas: Research Assistants will have additional capacity beyond what the math requires; they should not be allowed to become a bottleneck since they are the cheapest resource
Additional junior analysts will need to be hired to reach the 8 needed

categories.name: People and change management
ideas: Little resistance is expected from current analysts because Junior Analysts will no longer be doing work beneath them
Junior Analysts will have a manager trained in their field rather than reporting to the head of trading
Senior Analysts will focus on higher-value synthesis work

categories.name: Reporting lines
ideas: Junior Analysts should report to their respective Senior Analyst rather than directly to the head of trading
Senior Analysts report to the head of trading (unchanged)
Research Assistants are a shared resource and may report centrally

categories.name: Compensation
ideas: Compensation structures should reflect the new hierarchy and role clarity
Performance incentives should align with the fund's goal of maximizing returns
Clear career progression from Assistant → Jr. Analyst → Sr. Analyst aids retention

recommendation: Restructure the research team into four pods, each led by one Senior Analyst supported by two Junior Analysts, with one to two Research Assistants shared across all pods

This structure reflects the natural leverage ratio derived from the work allocation data: Senior Analysts focus on high-value synthesis (80% of synthesis work), Junior Analysts own analysis (80%), and Assistants handle data gathering (50%)
risks: The client currently only has 3 Junior Analysts and no Research Assistants, so significant hiring is required before the structure can function properly
Assistants risk being underutilized; care must be taken not to make them a bottleneck despite their low cost
Culture and morale risk if role boundaries are not clearly communicated during the transition
next_steps: Hire 5 additional Junior Analysts and 1–2 Research Assistants
Redefine job descriptions and escalation protocols for each level
Establish new reporting lines: Jr. Analysts report to their Sr. Analyst pod lead, not directly to the head of trading
Design compensation and incentive structures aligned with the new hierarchy and the fund's return-maximization goal
